# High-cardinality circuit structure and its exact nine-cap boundary

There is a simple positive structural result at high cap cardinality.
For \(n=d=2\), every circuit-compressed inclusion-minimal cover with
10, 11, or 12 original caps has four groups and a private original cap
in every group. At 12 caps the groups are disjoint full-rank triples;
at 11 caps at most one cap can be shared.

The tempting weaker general threshold \(N>2^n d\) is false: an exact
nine-cap example below forces three disjoint triples and a fourth
cross-triple with no private cap. All nine caps are essential on an
actual convex source, and their complementary polyhedron is bounded,
full-dimensional, and mixed-integer-free. Thus the positive result
starts at exactly the quantitatively relevant cardinality in
\(n=d=2\): strict budgets below \(\Gamma_2M/4=M/9\) require
\(N\ge10\) by the elementary union bound.

No critical-budget or below-OC claim is made for the nine-cap
counterexample. The positive combinatorial theorem is conditional
only on the stated circuit selection; it does not infer an objective
stress or a cap-mass inequality from private incidence alone.

## 1. An exact incidence and rank-defect budget

Let \(\{H_1,\ldots,H_N\}\) be an inclusion-minimal cover of a set \(S\).
Suppose \(s\le h\) selected groups cover \(S\), use only these original
caps, and have supports \(I_g\) of size \(k_g\le d+1\).
The groups may additionally be certified to cover whole fibers by
projected inequalities; that stronger property is not needed in
this counting argument. Let \(m_j\) be the number of groups containing
original cap \(j\).

Every original cap occurs: otherwise the selected union would be a
proper subcover. Therefore \(m_j\ge1\), and
\[
 \boxed{\;
 h(d+1)-N
 =(h-s)(d+1)+\sum_{g=1}^s(d+1-k_g)
                    +\sum_{j=1}^N(m_j-1).
 \;}                                                       \tag{1}
\]
This is the identity \(\sum_g k_g=\sum_j m_j\).
If every group is a minimal positive continuous-normal circuit,
its rank is \(r_g=k_g-1\). The middle term in (1) is then exactly
the total continuous-rank deficit \(\sum_g(d-r_g)\).
The last term is the total number of repeated cap occurrences.

Write \(\Delta=h(d+1)-N\). In particular:

- at most \(\Delta\) original caps are shared;
- at most \(\Delta\) groups are rank deficient;
- at most \(2\Delta\) groups meet any shared cap, since
  \(\sum_{j:m_j\ge2}m_j\le2\sum_j(m_j-1)\);
- every group has at least
  \(N-(s-1)(d+1)\) private original caps, when this number is positive.

For the last assertion, all nonprivate caps of a group occur in the
union of the other groups, which has at most \((s-1)(d+1)\) caps.
Equivalently, the original caps outside that union are precisely
the private caps of the given group.

Consequently
\[
 N>(h-1)(d+1)                                             \tag{2}
\]
forces \(s=h\) and at least one private cap in every group.
In this range the lower bound is \(d+1-\Delta\) private caps per
group, and at least \(h-2\Delta\) groups share no cap at all.

Take \(h=2^n\). The proposed condition \(N>hd\) implies (2) whenever
\(d\ge h-1\). For \(n=d=2\), (2) is \(N>9\). At \(N=10,11,12\)
it gives respectively at least one, two, or three private caps per
group. At \(N=12\), every term on the right of (1) is zero, so all
four groups have rank two and their triples are disjoint. At
\(N=11\), at most one original cap is repeated, and at least two
groups share no cap.

These conclusions do not require perturbing normals or discarding
compatibility constraints. They apply to any original-cap selection
with the stated count, including a selection supported by an
objective stress when such a stress has separately been proved.

## 2. Nine explicit halfspaces

Let \(z=(z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb R^2\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^2\).
Use continuous normals
\[
 u_0=(1,0),\quad u_1=(0,1),\quad u_2=(-1,-1).
\]
For \(g,i\in\{0,1,2\}\), set
\[
 H_{gi}=\{u_i\cdot x\ge b_{gi}(z)\},\qquad
 Q=\{u_i\cdot x\le b_{gi}(z)\ \text{for all }g,i\},
\]
where the affine threshold array is
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 g&b_{g0}&b_{g1}&b_{g2}\\ \hline
 0&-1+4z_1+4z_2&-1+4z_1+4z_2&-1+4z_1+4z_2\\
 1&3-4z_1+14z_2&7-8z_1-4z_2&3-4z_1\\
 2&3+14z_1-4z_2&3-4z_2&7-4z_1-8z_2 .
 \end{array}                                                \tag{3}
\]
All nine continuous normals are nonzero. The four base points are
\[
 A=(0,0),\quad B=(1,0),\quad C=(0,1),\quad D=(1,1).
\]
The threshold arrays there are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 &g=0&g=1&g=2\\ \hline
 A&(-1,-1,-1)&(3,7,3)&(3,3,7)\\
 B&(3,3,3)&(-1,-1,-1)&(17,3,3)\\
 C&(3,3,3)&(17,3,3)&(-1,-1,-1)\\
 D&(7,7,7)&(13,-5,-1)&(13,-1,-5).
 \end{array}                                                \tag{4}
\]

## 3. A bounded full-dimensional mixed-free polyhedron

Each original row \(g\) is a positive continuous-normal circuit.
There is also the cross-circuit
\[
 I_*=\{(0,0),(1,1),(2,2)\}.
 \]
Their threshold sums are respectively
\[
 \begin{split}
 L_0&=-3+12z_1+12z_2,\\
 L_1&=13-16z_1+10z_2,\\
 L_2&=13+10z_1-16z_2,\\
 L_*&=13-8z_1-8z_2.
 \end{split}                                                \tag{5}
\]
Every point of \(Q\) has all four sums nonnegative.
Writing \(s=z_1+z_2\), this implies
\[
 1/4\le s\le13/8,\qquad
 (16s-13)/26\le z_1\le(13+10s)/26.                          \tag{6}
\]
For an integer base, the first interval forces \(s=1\), while
the second becomes \(3/26\le z_1\le23/26\), which has no integer
point. Hence \(Q\cap(\mathbb Z^2\times\mathbb R^2)=\varnothing\).
The open outward caps therefore already cover the whole mixed
lattice.

The inequalities in (6) bound the base. On any bounded base set,
one row of the three inequalities with normals \(u_0,u_1,u_2\)
bounds the continuous coordinates, so \(Q\) is bounded.
At \(z=(1/2,1/2)\), every entry in (3) is positive (the minimum
is one), so \(x=0\) is a strict feasible point. Thus \(Q\) is
full-dimensional and nonempty.

## 4. Strict mixed witnesses make all nine caps essential

Let
\[
 v_0=(5/2,-5/4),\quad v_1=(-5/4,5/2),\quad
 v_2=(-5/4,-5/4).
\]
At \(v_i\), \(u_i\cdot v_i=5/2\) and both other normal values
are \(-5/4\).
For each cap \((g,i)\), use the witness \((P_g,v_i)\), where
\(P_0=A,P_1=B,P_2=C\). At that base its row has thresholds all
\(-1\), and every threshold in the other two rows is at least
three. Therefore the witness strictly satisfies just \(H_{gi}\).

Every original cap is indispensable even in the closed cover.
Equivalently, removing its inequality from \(Q\) gives a mixed
point strictly satisfying all the remaining inequalities.
Since \(Q\) also has a strict feasible point, these witnesses show
that all nine inequalities define actual facets.
This is not padding with redundant caps.

## 5. Four forced groups and no private cap in the fourth

Every minimal positive dependence among the nine continuous
normals takes exactly one copy of each of \(u_0,u_1,u_2\), with
equal weights. There are exactly \(3^3=27\) such circuits.
For a selected triple, its projected whole-fiber cover condition
is that its three thresholds sum to a nonpositive number.

At base \(A\), the unique circuit with nonpositive threshold sum
is the entire row 0: replacing even one of its \(-1\)'s by an
entry from another row gives sum at least \(-1-1+3=1\).
Likewise row 1 is uniquely required at \(B\), and row 2 at \(C\).

At \(D\), the unique circuit with nonpositive sum is \(I_*\).
Indeed its values are \((7,-5,-5)\), of sum \(-3\). Replacing
either \(-5\) by the next available value \(-1\) gives sum one;
replacing the first value seven by thirteen gives sum three.
All further replacements only increase the sum.

Consequently any projected-cover selection for these four bases
must contain exactly these four required circuits before adding
any others. The first three disjoint rows already contain all
nine original caps. The fourth circuit has no private original
cap. Four groups do cover every integer base, by (6).

Here \(N=9>2^2\cdot2=8\), disproving the proposed threshold
\(N>2^n d\). The defect identity (1) is exact: all four groups
have full continuous rank, and the entire deficit
\(\Delta=4\cdot3-9=3\) is spent on the three repeated
cross-circuit cap occurrences.

The strict signs also make the construction robust. Under
sufficiently small rational perturbations of the nine normals
and thresholds, the same 27 triple supports remain the only
minimal positive circuits: one-from-each-direction triples stay
positive, and all other triples remain strictly separated from
zero in their convex hull. Their normalized weights vary
continuously. The four unique projected-cover choices at the
four bases, the nine essential witnesses, and the strict feasible
point persist. Bounded polyhedron continuity and the positive
distance from the compact \(Q\) to the mixed lattice preserve
mixed freeness. The four selected projected inequalities in (6)
also define a bounded integer-free polygon; its positive distance
from the integer lattice and the same continuity argument preserve
the four-group global cover. Thus the parallel copies of the original normals
are not essential to the obstruction; small generic rational
perturbations may remove their parallelism.

## 6. Exact actual source and budget calibration

Set \(K=\operatorname{conv}\{v_0,v_1,v_2\}\),
\(\delta=1/100\), and \(E=[-\delta,\delta]^2\). Let
\[
 C_{\rm src}=\operatorname{conv}
 \bigl((\{A,B,C\}\times K)\cup(\{D\}\times E)\bigr).            \tag{7}
\]
Its projection is the binary square. A convex combination at any
binary vertex uses only that vertex's source fiber. Thus (7) has
exactly the four prescribed integer fibers, all full-dimensional.
It is a full-dimensional compact convex body and equals the hull
of its actual mixed source.
Every witness in Section 4 has a positive-area neighborhood within
its triangle belonging only to its own cap. Hence all nine caps
remain essential on this actual source.

For completeness the cap masses can be computed exactly. The
triangle has area \(V_K=225/32\); each own cap at threshold
\(-1\) has area
\[
 V_K(14/15)^2=49/8.
\]
All other triangle fibers are strictly excluded. At \(D\),
the row-0 caps and the direction-0 caps of rows 1 and 2 exclude
the square; the remaining four caps capture its full area
\(4\delta^2=1/2500\). Thus every original cap has mass either
\(49/8\) or \(49/8+1/2500\), while
\[
 M=675/32+1/2500.
\]
This is an actual strict-budget depth-region cover for any
threshold between the largest displayed cap mass and \(M\).

Its actual maximum absolute depth is \(25/8\). Each binary base
is exposed, so a finite oblique tilt isolates any own-fiber cap.
The triangle centroids have own depth
\(\Gamma_2 V_K=25/8\), which is also the ordinary maximum of
a triangle; the square's own maximum is only \(1/5000\).
The matching lower bounds use the own fiber. Therefore the
displayed nine-cap budgets are not critical for this source,
and the normalized actual depth is above the OC target.

## 7. What is usable at the below-target cardinalities

For \(n=d=2\), a hypothetical strict cover with every cap mass
below \(M/9\) needs at least ten distinct caps. If such an
inclusion-minimal original cover admits a selection of at most
four minimal positive circuits from its own caps, the positive
private-cap conclusion in Section 1 is automatic.
At eleven or twelve caps it gives the additional overlap/rank
restrictions stated there.

The existence of such an original-cap circuit selection must
still be supplied by its actual covering model. An arbitrary
cover of the bounded source is not assumed to cover entire
fiber spaces, and the strict auxiliary-polyhedron construction
may replace caps. Nor does private incidence itself provide
the missing sharp multiplier or volume estimate.
This is a precise high-cardinality invariant and its exact
nine-cap boundary, not a proof of OC.
